brief.situation: 10:15 in an inpatient rehabilitation gym. You are the neurologic physical therapist. Mr. Okonkwo, 29, has a complete T4 spinal cord injury; he has been in a standing frame for 10 minutes. His usual sitting blood pressure is about 100/64.
handover: He says, 'My head's pounding, and I'm sweating up top.' His face is flushed.
He has an indwelling urinary catheter; his leg bag is strapped to his calf under his compression stockings and abdominal binder.

Rehab unit protocol for autonomic dysreflexia: sit upright with legs down, loosen anything tight, check the catheter tubing for kinks and the bag, recheck blood pressure every 2-5 minutes, and call the nurse and physician at once; drugs are given by the nurse on the physician's order.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What is happening to Mr. Okonkwo, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: With a T4 injury, a sudden rise in blood pressure to 172/104, a pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the injury and a slow pulse are autonomic dysreflexia, most often from the bladder.
parts.modelAnswer: It's autonomic dysreflexia. He's T4, his pressure's 70 over baseline, he has a pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the level, and a slow pulse. The bladder's the usual cause.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stops, sits him upright with legs down, loosens the binder and stockings, checks the catheter tubing and bag (finding the kink), rechecks blood pressure every few minutes and calls the nurse and physician.
parts.modelAnswer: Out of the frame, sit him up with his legs down, loosen everything, trace the catheter and fix the kink, recheck his pressure every few minutes, and call the nurse and doctor.

bleed.headline: Hypertensive emergency
bleed.body: A T6-or-above injury with a sudden rise in pressure and a pounding headache is autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, legs down, loosen, find the trigger (the bladder first), and call.

safe.headline: Trigger found and removed
safe.body: You took his pressure, sat him up, loosened his clothing, found the kinked catheter and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

safeGaps.headline: Resolved, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Check whether he was sat up or laid flat, how soon you called, and whether you went to the bladder first.

scoring.modelReasoning: In injuries at or above T6, a noxious stimulus below the injury (most often bladder distension or a kinked catheter) triggers autonomic dysreflexia: a sudden rise in blood pressure, headache, flushing and sweating above the injury, and reflex bradycardia. Sit him upright with legs down, loosen restrictive clothing, monitor blood pressure every few minutes, survey the causes starting with the bladder (here a kinked catheter under the stocking strap), and call the nurse and physician; drugs follow if the pressure stays high.
